clue.text: Lament rise of fear in the party

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters are read from the bottom upwards
one word is put inside the other, sitting in it as a filling

parts.note: Lib is short for the Liberal party
awe is reverential fear

explanation.surface: A cry of grief over growing alarm within a political party.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue rise applies to the whole assembled word, not just to fear, so the container is built first and then turned upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To bewail something is to grieve over it loudly, a literary synonym for mourn or lament.

clue.text: Whereof George is 15

parts.note: surface reading: a riddle about England's patron saint and a number; setter's reading: 15 across is a senior archbishop, and George Carey held that office; the answer completes his title

explanation.walkthrough: The 15 refers to the answer at 15 across. George Carey, Archbishop of Canterbury when this was set, was Primate of this whole country.
explanation.definitionFit: The Archbishop of Canterbury's formal title is Primate of All England, so this is the realm over which he holds that rank.

clue.text: They lean precariously in Somerset

definitions.note: a place found in Somerset, while the answer is its name

indicators.note: things set up precariously are unstable and liable to topple into a different arrangement

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: Somerset folk, or perhaps its trees or towers, tilting at alarming angles.
explanation.walkthrough: Athelney is the marshy isle in Somerset where King Alfred hid from the Danes and, by legend, burnt the cakes.
explanation.definitionFit: Athelney is a village and former island on the Somerset Levels in south-west England, famous for its Alfred connection.

clue.text: Diner consumes Sunday feast

indicators.note: whatever is consumed ends up inside the eater, so one piece is swallowed by the other

parts.note: a diner is someone who eats
S is the abbreviation for Sunday

explanation.surface: Someone eating a big Sunday dinner.
explanation.definitionFit: Easter is a major Christian festival, and feast is used for any religious festival day in the church calendar.

clue.text: Covering letter?

parts.note: surface reading: the explanatory note sent with a job application; setter's reading: the paper item that literally covers a letter in the post

explanation.definitionFit: An envelope is the paper wrapper in which mail is sealed, so it physically covers what is posted.

clue.text: Logis are inappropriate accommodation for concubines

indicators.note: something inappropriate is out of place, so these letters must be moved into proper places

parts.note: logis together with are supplies the letters

explanation.surface: Logis, French lodgings, are judged unsuitable for housing a sultan's concubines.
explanation.walkthrough: The fodder is logis plus the are that also forms part of the indicator phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: A seraglio is the women's quarters of an Ottoman palace, a harem where wives and concubines lived.

clue.text: Excess of dubious help to artist

indicators.note: dubious suggests something doubtful and not right, so the letters are put into another order

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged
RA is a Royal Academician, a standard artist

explanation.surface: Too much questionable assistance given to a painter.
explanation.definitionFit: A plethora is an overabundance, more of something than is needed or wanted.

clue.text: Type of ring to give a friend?

parts.note: a ring is round like the letter O
a pal is a friend

explanation.surface: Wondering what sort of ring to present to a friend.
explanation.walkthrough: The word ring does double duty: part of the definition and also the source of O.
explanation.definitionFit: An opal is a gemstone often set in rings, so an opal ring is one kind of ring.

clue.text: Like have a degree in sums

definitions.note: sums looks like a plural noun but works as a third-person verb, matching the answer's verb form

indicators.note: to have something is to hold it, so the first word holds the other inside

parts.note: as means like, in a comparison
DD is a Doctor of Divinity degree

explanation.surface: Someone who holds a mathematics degree.
explanation.walkthrough: Read sums as a verb, not as arithmetic problems.
explanation.definitionFit: To sum figures is to total them, which is exactly what it means to add them.

clue.text: Party minister backed in speech

definitions.note: an adverbial phrase, while the answer is an adjective meaning spoken

indicators.note: backed means put into reverse, so the pair is read from right to left

parts.note: Lab is short for the Labour party
a minister of religion is a Rev, short for Reverend

explanation.surface: A party politician is supported when giving a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A verbal agreement or warning is one given in spoken words rather than in writing.

clue.text: Old resistance fighter given prize by governor

parts.note: HE is His Excellency, the title of a colonial governor
a reward is a prize

explanation.surface: A veteran partisan receiving a medal from a colonial governor.
explanation.walkthrough: By places the governor's letters beside the prize, and here they come first.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereward the Wake led English resistance against the Norman conquerors from the Fens around Ely in 1070.

clue.text: Bar terms

parts.note: surface reading: the conditions of a pub, or the words used over a drink; setter's reading: the Bar is the legal profession, so these are the words lawyers use

explanation.definitionFit: Barristers are called to the Bar, and the specialised vocabulary of law courts is known by this phrase.

clue.text: A mean fellow is not unusual

definitions.note: an adjective phrase, while the answer is a noun for the person who is not unusual

parts.note: an average is a mean in statistics
a fellow is a man

explanation.surface: A stingy fellow is a common sight.
explanation.walkthrough: Mean looks like stingy, but it is the statistical mean.
explanation.definitionFit: The average man is the typical ordinary person, someone with nothing out of the ordinary about him.

clue.text: Stress breaking up ship; mate's lost heart

indicators.note: something broken up falls apart into pieces that can be reassembled differently

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: losing the heart means the central letter of that word goes missing

parts.note: the possessive read as plain letters; its middle letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A shipwreck in which the mate is in despair.
explanation.walkthrough: MATES loses its central T to leave MAES, and those letters join SHIP to be rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Emphasis and stress both mean the special importance or force given to a word or idea.

clue.text: Lightweight journal?

parts.note: surface reading: a trivial magazine with no serious content; setter's reading: boxing has flyweights, and the sticky sheet that traps insects is a paper named after them

explanation.definitionFit: Flypaper is a sticky strip hung up to trap insects, punningly a paper for the smallest weight class.

clue.text: Model left part-time involvement with church dignitary

indicators.note: something involved is tangled, so the remaining letters are knotted into a new order
left here means departed from, so one letter goes out of the longer word

parts.note: taken as written, without the hyphen
the Model T was Ford's famous car, so model can give T

explanation.surface: A fashion model has quit a part-time role connected with a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: One T departs from PARTTIME, leaving PARTIME to be rearranged. Model looks like a fashion model but stands for the Model T.
explanation.definitionFit: A primate is an archbishop, the senior bishop of a province or country, and so a high church dignitary.

clue.text: Pioneer of the web site?

parts.note: surface reading: someone who created an early internet site; setter's reading: the original builder of webs, long before the internet, is a spinner of silk

explanation.definitionFit: Spiders belong to the class of eight-legged creatures that includes scorpions and mites, and they spun webs first.

clue.text: Some baby, small enough to be bottomless

indicators.note: some means only a portion, so the letters are a run taken from within the following words

parts.note: the run spans the end of the first word and all of the second

explanation.surface: An infant so tiny it seems to have no bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: Abysmal originally meant like an abyss, immeasurably deep, hence having no bottom at all.

clue.text: Titanic orchestra playing to order?

parts.note: an orchestra is a band, with the article
a show that is playing is on
the Titanic was a ship

explanation.surface: The band famously played on as the Titanic sank.
explanation.walkthrough: The story goes that the Titanic's musicians kept playing while the liner went down.
explanation.definitionFit: Abandon ship is the command given when a vessel is sinking, telling everyone aboard to get off.

clue.text: Donkey and another old one

indicators.note: another means a different version, so the letters of old one are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written as anagram fodder
taken as written

explanation.surface: An old donkey is joined by a second old animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Donkey' is a fool here, not the animal.
explanation.definitionFit: A donkey and a noodle are both informal words for a silly person.

clue.text: Father participates in Hebrew Sabbath observance

indicators.note: what participates in something forms part of it, so the letters lie inside the next word

parts.note: the run sits between the first and last two letters

explanation.surface: A father joining in the Jewish day of rest.
explanation.walkthrough: Hebrew and observance only dress the surface; they also hint that the word is Semitic.
explanation.definitionFit: Abba is the Aramaic and Hebrew word for father, used in the New Testament as a form of address to God.

clue.text: Trick of speaking at length

indicators.note: speaking means we go by how the word is said, not how it is written

parts.note: a while is a length of time

explanation.surface: A trick of talking for a long time.
explanation.definitionFit: A wile is a crafty stratagem or ruse meant to deceive or entice someone.

clue.text: Sea captain — not half a terrible wretch

parts.note: Captain William Bligh commanded HMS Bounty at the time of the mutiny

indicators.note: not half means less than half of the word terrible, its first few letters

explanation.surface: A sea captain who was awful, but not half as bad as a true scoundrel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not half' takes fewer than half the letters of 'terrible': its first three, TER.
explanation.definitionFit: A blighter is an informal British word for a contemptible or unfortunate person, a wretch.

clue.text: Get away — piss off, in common parlance

parts.note: to go is to get away

indicators.note: off suggests something gone wrong or out of order, so those letters are mixed up

parts.note: the letters to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A crude way of telling someone to go away.
explanation.definitionFit: Gossip is idle everyday talk about others, the ordinary chatter of common speech.

clue.text: Little by little, a man takes over — he's over there

indicators.note: taking over something means absorbing it, so the outer word swallows the other

parts.note: taken as written
Eric, or Little by Little is a Victorian school story by Dean Farrar

explanation.surface: Gradually, a man assumes control.
explanation.walkthrough: Little by little looks like gradually, but it is the subtitle of a famous Victorian novel about a boy named Eric.
explanation.definitionFit: From a British viewpoint a citizen of the United States lives across the Atlantic, over there.

clue.text: Inferior competitor follows Cambridge lead — but not so far behind

indicators.note: the lead of a word is its front, so only its opening letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter
a loser is a competitor who is beaten

explanation.surface: A poor rival trails Cambridge in a boat race, yet narrows the gap.
explanation.definitionFit: Closer is the comparative of near, so it describes something at a shorter distance behind.
